title: Architecture standards: Crosscutting guidelines and ADR process
author: Sofia Reynolds
content:
## Architecture & Standards — Crosscutting Guidelines

Short intro:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical crosscutting architecture and engineering standards: API standards, coding standards, infrastructure standards, model-serving standards, observability standards, performance SLOs, and the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process. It is intended as the centralized reference for design reviews, PRs, and operational runbooks. Owners and reviewers should keep this page up to date; see the "Related pages" section for subsystem-level guidance.

---

## Scope
Applicable to: all backend services (hosted API, dedicated control plane, private deployments), inference runtime components, and platform tooling maintained by Engineering. Not a replacement for team-level runbooks; teams must implement additional constraints to meet product SLAs and regulatory requirements.

## High-level principles
- Single source of truth: API compatibility and schema changes must be documented via ADRs and API versioning guidances.
- Backwards compatibility by default: prefer additive changes and deprecation windows.
- Observable by design: every service must emit structured traces, metrics and request-level logs.
- Cost-awareness: model-serving decisions should include unit-cost impact (tokens / GPU-sec) and perf tradeoffs.
- Ownership: each standard lists a named owning team and an on-call rotation for breaches.

---

## 1) API standards (owner: eng-developer-experience)
Purpose: ensure stable, idiomatic, and versioned APIs for customers and internal services.

Key rules:
1. Use RESTful, JSON-over-HTTPS for external APIs; internal RPC may use gRPC but must provide HTTP gateways for external integrations.
2. Versioning: follow URL versioning (/v1/ or /v2/). Breaking changes require an ADR and a 90-day deprecation window for hosted customers; enterprise/private customers get 6 months by contract.
3. Schema evolution: additive fields only; enums must include a fallback "UNKNOWN" value. Avoid nullable overloading.
4. Error model: use standard JSON error object: {
   "code": "string",
   "message": "string",
   "details": { /* freeform */ }
}
5. Rate-limiting and quotas: endpoints must document rate limits and response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.
6. Authentication: OAuth2 bearer tokens for external APIs; mutual TLS optional for private deployments.

Example request/response snippet:
``
POST /v1/generate
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "model": "redwood/text-2b",
  "input": "Summarize the quarterly results",
  "max_tokens": 256
}
``

Response: 200 OK with streaming support (Transfer-Encoding: chunked) and final JSON envelope.

API review checklist (must be completed before merging):
- [ ] API contract (OpenAPI spec) added to repo.
- [ ] Backwards compatibility verified.
- [ ] Request/response size and rate limits documented.
- [ ] Cost estimate for per-request unit economics included.

---

## 2) Coding standards (owner: eng-platform)
Purpose: consistent code quality, security hygiene, and maintainability.

Rules and tooling:
- Languages and style: follow language-specific style guides. For Python use Black + isort + pytype; for Go use gofmt + govet; for Rust use rustfmt + clippy.
- Linting and CI: all PRs must pass lint, unit tests, and static analysis. Hidden test owners must be included for infra changes.
- Security: run SAST (Semgrep) and dependency scanning; any high/critical findings must be triaged within 48 hours.
- Secrets: forbid secrets in repos; use Secret Manager + KMS. PRs that attempt to add plaintext secrets are blocked by pre-commit hooks.
- API clients: generated from OpenAPI / protobuf specs; do not hand-author public SDK interfaces without a design RFC.

Code review expectations:
- 2 approvers required for production-impacting PRs (>3 files or touching runtime scheduling).
- Add a test plan and QA steps in the PR description.

Example pre-commit hook (Python):
``
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/psf/black
    rev: 23.7.0
    hooks:
      - id: black
``

---

## 3) Infrastructure standards (owner: eng-infra)
Purpose: secure, scalable cloud infrastructure for hosted and private deployments.

Key constraints:
- IaC: Terraform is the canonical tool; modules published under infra/terraform-modules. Changes to shared modules must go through module-owner review.
- Environments: prod, staging, canary, dev. Canary traffic must be 0.5%-1% by default for rollout experiments.
- Networking: VPCs per-customer for Private; cross-account IAM roles for Dedicated control plane. Enforce least privilege for all IAM roles.
- Secrets and keys: KMS for key management; HSM for top-tier enterprise customers.
- Backups and retention: DB backups daily, 30-day retention by default; PII needs policy-based retention.

Minimal production guardrails table:
| Area | Requirement | Threshold/Setting |
|------|-------------|------------------|
| Availability | Multi-AZ for stateful services | RPO < 1h, RTO < 2h |
| Scaling | Autoscaling groups + scheduled scale | Target CPU/GPU util 60-75% |
| Throttling | API gateway per-customer quotas | configurable per-customer |

Runbook links: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks and per-service runbook must include restore steps.

---

## 4) Model-serving standards (owner: eng-serving-runtime)
Purpose: ensure predictable latency, cost, and correctness for model inference.

Core guidance:
- Model catalog: all models served must be registered in the catalog with artifact hash, quantization profile, and validated evals (quality checks).
- Quantization: prefer 8-bit quantized weights for CPU-bound services; float16/FP8 for GPU when validated. Include regression tests in eval harness.
- Deployment primitives: support variant routing (e.g., model-v1-fast, model-v1-accurate). Default rollout policy: canary 5% -> 25% -> 100% over a 24-72 hour window depending on risk.
- KV cache & batching: runtime must expose tuning knobs; teams should publish expected sequence length distribution and target P99 latency.

Service SLOs (model-serving):
- Availability: 99.9% monthly for API endpoints backed by dedicated Capacity.
- Latency: P95 < 120ms for small context requests (<256 tokens) on dedicated pools; P99 < 300ms across hosted tiers.
- Error budget: 0.1% monthly. Exceeding error budget triggers Reliability Initiative (see SRE runbooks).

Model rollout checklist:
1. Add model to catalog with metadata (name, version, checksum, quantization profile, eval results).
2. Run automated evals against production prompt set.
3. Deploy to canary pool (5% traffic) and monitor: latency, token throughput, quality regressions.
4. If no regression in 24h, advance to 25% for 24h then 100%.

---

## 5) Observability standards (owner: eng-platform)
Purpose: deterministic monitoring and rapid diagnosis.

Requirements:
- Metrics: all services must export the three golden signals (latency, error rate, throughput) plus model-specific metrics (tokens/sec, active KV cache hit rate, batch size). Use Prometheus exposition where feasible.
- Tracing: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry. Root spans must include request_id, model_id, and route. Trace sampling: 1% by default; increase to 100% for canary and incidents.
- Logs: structured JSON logs. Correlate logs with trace ids and request ids. Sensitive fields must be redacted at source.
- Dashboards: per-service SLO dashboard in Grafana and an aggregated product-level dashboard in Redwood Console.

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- P99 latency increase > 30% over baseline for 5m -> P1 (oncall).
- Error rate > 0.5% sustained for 10m -> P1.
- KV cache hit rate < 60% and cost increases -> P2.

---

## 6) Performance standards & benchmarks (owner: eng-serving-runtime)
Purpose: consistent performance evaluation and acceptance criteria for changes.

Benchmarks and methodology:
- Use the standardized benchmarking harness under applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness. Benchmarks must report: tokens/sec, latency percentiles (P50/P95/P99), GPU utilization, memory, and per-token cost.
- Benchmark environments must be reproducible and recorded with commit hash, hardware SKU, kernel version, driver version, and kernel flags.

Minimum acceptance criteria for runtime changes:
- Non-regressive: all critical benchmarks for target models must not regress more than 3% on P95 latency and 5% on tokens/sec unless explicitly approved in an ADR.
- Load safety: new scheduling or batching logic must be tested under 2x expected concurrency and must not increase median CPU/GPU utilization by >10% unless offset by throughput gains.

Example benchmark summary table (text):
| Model | HW | P95 Lat (ms) | Tokens/sec | Notes |
|-------|----|--------------:|-----------:|-------|
| redwood/text-2b | A100-80GB | 110 | 12k | quantized int8 |

---

## 7) ADR process (owner: eng-architecture)
Purpose: formalize architectural decisions and their rationale so future engineers can understand tradeoffs.

When to write an ADR:
- Any design that affects service interfaces, deployment topology, data schema, security boundaries, or substantially changes cost or latency assumptions.

ADR template (short form) — include as the file header for every ADR:
- Title: short descriptive title
- Status: proposed | accepted | superseded | deprecated
- Context: background and constraints
- Decision: what we decided and why
- Consequences: operational, cost, security implications
- Owners: author and reviewers
- Date: YYYY-MM-DD

Procedure:
1. Draft ADR in the arch repo under docs/adrs/ with the template. Use Markdown and include links to relevant benchmarks, cost estimates, and diagrams.
2. Assign reviewers from affected teams (API, infra, runtime, SRE).
3. At least one cross-team review meeting when the ADR affects multiple subsystems.
4. Merge after reviewers sign off; set status to "accepted" and link to any follow-up tickets.
5. Store canonical ADR in Confluence with a short summary and link to the repo file.

Example accepted ADR summary:
- Title: Use quantized int8 for CPU-bound inference
- Status: accepted
- Context: reduce cost for lower-throughput private customers while maintaining accuracy
- Decision: adopt int8 quantization with mandatory eval guardrails and an opt-out for customers who require float32
- Consequences: ~3x reduction in inference cost on CPU, requires additional regression tests and updated model catalog metadata

---

## Ownership and governance
- Owners: each standard section lists an owner team. The architecture guild coordinates cross-team reviews monthly.
- Exceptions: request exceptions via the Risk & Exceptions process in security-and-compliance. Exceptions must include compensating controls, a TTL (max 90 days), and an owner.

## Appendix: quick checklists
- New public API: create OpenAPI spec, write migration plan, file ADR if breaking.
- New model: register in catalog, attach eval artifacts, follow rollout checklist.
- Infra module change: bump module version, run dependent-service tests, notify module consumers.

---

If you find gaps or need clarification, open a PR against this page or ping the architecture guild: #arch-guild in Slack.
